sources.title: Jensen Huang rompe su silencio tras dejar NVIDIA: «Sería un honor regresar como CEO»
sources.text: Cada día que pasa se escribe un nuevo capítulo del culebrón por la salida de Jensen Huang como presidente y CEO de NVIDIA . El ejecutivo aprovechó hoy su perfil en X (Twitter) para pronunciarse en público por primera vez desde su renuncia a la conducción de la empresa . En su comunicado no solo reconoció sus errores, sino que también mostró su interés por volver a liderar la compañía que cofundó en 1993 . El mensaje de Jensen Huang marca todos los casilleros de lo que se podría esperar de un discurso de arrepentimiento . El exCEO de NVIDIA agradeció las muestras de cariño de quienes se comunicaron con él en los últimos días, como también de quienes pidieron por su regreso al gigante verde. Asimismo, celebró su historia como inmigrante y las posibilidades que le abrió Estados Unidos desde su llegada, hizo un mea culpa de su comportamiento, se comprometió a colaborar con la investigación sobre su accionar, le pidió disculpas a su familia y sentó las bases para un potencial vuelta al rol principal de la empresa. Las repercusiones del primer mensaje público de Jensen Huang tras renunciar a NVIDIA no se hicieron esperar. Al momento de redacción de este artículo, el posteo acumula más de 39.000 republicaciones y 238.000 likes . No quedan dudas de que sus palabras eran las más codiciadas, especialmente tras un anuncio de salida de la compañía que no incluyó ningún comentario de su parte. A continuación, el mensaje completo que publicó Jensen Huang en X (Twitter), traducido al español: Durante la última semana, me he sentido profundamente conmovido por el cariño y el apoyo de amigos, colegas del sector y personas a las que ni siquiera conozco. Gracias a todos los que han mostrado tanta amabilidad hacia mí y mi familia. Significa muchísimo para mí. Llegué a Estados Unidos hace 53 años, y convertirme en ciudadano estadounidense fue uno de los mayores regalos y uno de los momentos de mayor orgullo de mi vida. NVIDIA fue el proyecto de mi vida. Haber contribuido, junto a mis colegas, a convertirla en la empresa que es hoy ha sido un privilegio y un honor. Solo en Estados Unidos podría haber surgido una compañía como NVIDIA. Amo a nuestro país y amo a NVIDIA. No estuve a la altura de los estándares que se esperan de todos en NVIDIA, y he cometido errores graves en mi vida personal. He causado problemas a la Junta Directiva, algo de lo que me arrepiento profundamente. Asumo la total responsabilidad por mis errores y me comprometo a colaborar con la investigación independiente que está llevando a cabo la Junta. Desde mi salida, he recibido numerosas peticiones por parte de empleados, inversores, socios comerciales y clientes de NVIDIA para que regrese como CEO. Muchos siguen contactándome directamente mientras la empresa navega por complejas dinámicas tecnológicas, de mercado, competitivas y geopolíticas. NVIDIA es una empresa excepcional, de esas que solo aparecen una vez por generación. Si la Junta Directiva considera que mi regreso favorece los intereses de nuestros accionistas, empleados, la propia compañía y Estados Unidos, sería un honor atender estas peticiones y volver a ocupar el cargo de CEO. Gracias, de nuevo, a todos los que me han hecho llegar sus buenos deseos. Me siento profundamente conmovido por su apoyo. A mi familia: los amo, y dedicaré el resto de mi vida a ser digno de su cariño. Queda claro que Jensen Huang no ha tirado la toalla de forma definitiva con NVIDIA . Tras el escándalo por sus aventuras con la supuesta espía china Alice Huang y con la ejecutiva Kimberly Powell, la renuncia del empresario parecía ser el abrupto final de una historia hasta aquí plagada de éxitos. Pero unos pocos días le han bastado para tratar de recuperar el trono perdido. Un reciente reporte de Financial Times indicaba que Huang supuestamente había manifestado su deseo de regresar a NVIDIA a personas de confianza. La compañía ya ha puesta en marcha la búsqueda de un sucesor y todo apunta a que el Consejo de Administración prefiere dar vuelta la página antes que darle una segunda oportunidad al exCEO. Con el mensaje de hoy, Jensen Huang pone su destino en manos de la Junta Directiva . Y si bien a primera vista puede parecer un gesto de nobleza y colaboración, también impone una gran presión sobre los integrantes de la mesa . Después de todo, si eligen a otro CEO y no se logran los resultados esperados, la culpa será de ellos. El timing del mensaje de Jensen Huang tampoco es casual. La publicación se da justo el mismo día en que NVIDIA presentará los resultados financieros del último trimestre. Wall Street proyecta cifras de ventas que dupliquen las del trimestre previo, aunque la verdadera atención estará en lo que responda Colette Kress , la CEO interina, a las consultas de los inversores y accionistas. Con el comunicado de Huang en boca de todos, es lógico pensar en un bombardeo de preguntas sobre si la empresa analiza o no traerlo de regreso. Pase lo que pase, se esperan reacciones drásticas (para bien o para mal) en el valor de la acción del gigante verde.

sources.name: Xataka
sources.title: Jensen Huang rompe su silencio tras dimitir: “Sería un honor volver como CEO de NVIDIA”
sources.text: Jensen Huang ha dicho que sería “un honor” volver a dirigir NVIDIA si el consejo se lo pide . Es su primera declaración pública desde que dimitió la semana pasada. Su salida llegó tras conocerse varias relaciones extramatrimoniales: una con una empleada y otra con Alice Huang, una mujer a la que la inteligencia estadounidense investiga como posible activo de China. Qué ha dicho . El comunicado es breve, lo ha publicado en X y tiene dos partes: Entre líneas . El último de la lista es Estados Unidos, y eso va por Donald Trump. El lunes, el presidente dijo que “no le importaría” ver a Huang de vuelta y que este “ha aprendido una gran lección”. Huang se está apalancando en una presión que ya estaba ahí antes del comunicado. Hay una petición firmada por casi 200.000 empleados , la carta de un alto directivo al presidente del consejo, Harvey Jones; y el apoyo de Elon Musk. El mercado también lo ha notado: las acciones han recuperado lo que habían perdido en el día en cuanto el WSJ adelantó el comunicado. Sí, pero . Según el WSJ y CNN , el consejo no está pensando en readmitirle. Va en dirección contraria: el martes creó un comité que vigilará la seguridad nacional y el cumplimiento de los controles de exportación. Colette Kress sigue como CEO interina mientras se buscan candidatos dentro y fuera de la empresa. Y ahora qué . El 1 de diciembre, Huang declarará a puerta cerrada ante tres comités de la Cámara de Representantes, entre ellos el de Inteligencia. Al día siguiente lo hará el director jurídico de NVIDIA, Tim Teter. Las transcripciones podrán hacerse públicas más tarde y desde luego que por aquí las seguiremos con atención. En Xataka | Nvidia es el Super Glue de la industria de la IA. Sin Huang al frente, temen que sea pegamento de barra

stories.title: With Jensen Huang gone, Colette Kress shows Nvidia is still at the center of AI
stories.summary: In her first earnings report as interim CEO, Nvidia's Colette Kress calmed investors' nerves, at least for the moment.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: With Jensen Huang gone, Colette Kress shows Nvidia is still at the center of AI
sources.text: Five days after Nvidia 's Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded 33 years ago under a cloud of scandal, a nervous base of shareholders eagerly awaited Colette Kress' first public appearance as interim CEO. Following Nvidia's better-than-expected earnings report on Tuesday, Kress offered some relief to Wall Street, at least temporarily, by proclaiming on the call with analysts that customers are still fully onboard and that there's no slippage in demand. She said leadership from Nvidia's most important supplier, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company , visited company offices this week. "We've engaged with our customers, we've engaged with our suppliers, our partners, they're all 100% behind us," Kress said on the call. "Customers have expressed their support to the business outlook and helping us through that." While Huang was a singular figure in artificial intelligence with a commanding presence across the globe, Nvidia is still at the center of the AI ecosystem. Customers ranging from hyperscalers and neoclouds to frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic remain in persistent need of its technology and capital. Nvidia shares climbed almost 5% in extended trading on Tuesday after the chipmaker's better-than-expected earnings and strong guidance. That still leaves the stock in a deep slump after a 24% drop so far this month, driven by broad concerns about a slowdown in the AI buildout, a political handoff in Washington, D.C., and the turmoil at the top of the company. Despite all those headwinds and what Nvidia called the "unexpected transition" in leadership, the business is still booming. Revenue more than doubled in the latest quarter to $115.84 billion, and Nvidia projects roughly 90% growth in the current period to about $130 billion. More importantly, Kress said the 70% growth forecast for next year that was offered over the summer is actually too low. Now the projection is 75%. That's for a company that's seen revenue multiply by about 15-fold since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022. While Huang is gone, "demand did not leave with him," Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives said in a note after the report. Kress maintained her optimistic tone in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer after the call. "The most important thing that we have been seeing is continuing growth in terms of the demand that's out there," she said. Kress also said on the call that Nvidia's stepped-up buybacks, announced in September, are still on track, confirming that the board had added $150 billion to the company's authorization for share repurchases. It's not all on Kress. The consistent message throughout the earnings call was that Nvidia is preparing for life after Huang. Harvey Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia's board, opened by saying that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms," the first time the board had given a reason for his removal. A day earlier, CNBC reported that Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Kress said on the call that it's "business as usual." In a statement, she said the company's roadmap is "on track," indicating that there haven't been any changes to future chips and systems currently in development. Nvidia said that the Vera Rubin AI system is off to an "extraordinary start," selling $20 billion in the latest quarter. But Kress did signal a slight change to the company's willingness to backstop certain projects, and said Nvidia is being "disciplined" with how it's thinking about financing startups. "There's a lot of discussion internally with a lot of the teams on what we think are the best ones that we want to do," Kress told Cramer. "We're going to continue down that path to make sure we choose the right investments for us to work through going forward," Nvidia said its quarterly filing would be published in the "coming weeks," whereas it normally lands on the same day as earnings. On the call, neither Kress nor Jones addressed an avalanche of investigations and hearings in Washington looking into allegations that Nvidia was boosting revenue by selling chips to companies that are passthroughs for buyers in China. China only came up twice during the call. Kress said Nvidia had sold about $2.4 billion worth of approved data center products to China during the quarter, and that Nvidia had stopped selling licensed Hopper chips to China. Kress also noted that new trade rules released by the U.S. Commerce Department will cut off Chinese access to renting Nvidia chips. "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us and employees are committed," Kress said when signing off the call. "We've got this." WATCH: Nvidia out with 'very solid report'

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Nvidia’s Board Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang
sources.text: As Nvidia reported its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the company’s financial performance was overshadowed by the drama surrounding its former CEO . And Nvidia’s board made one thing clear right off the bat: Jensen Huang isn’t coming back . At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “groundbreaking technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said. Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and that the work can be done in the current environment.” Jones added that the Nvidia board is taking the search for a new CEO “very seriously” and is considering both internal and external candidates. National security dynamics are changing the chip industry, Jones said, and “our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough. We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.” One recurring theme emerged from the earnings call, aside from the Huang saga: Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains as strong as ever. Kress said that Nvidia expects that it will keep growing throughout 2027 and into 2028, fueled by the rise of agentic AI. Less than a week after Huang resigned as chief executive, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended on October 25. That exceeded analysts’ expectations of roughly $109 billion and was nearly double the revenue reported in the same quarter a year ago. The vast majority of Nvidia’s revenue came from its data center business, which generated $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year ago. Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, who had served as an executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider called Megaspeed. Then, reports emerged that Nvidia’s longtime leader additionally had an affair with one of his direct reports; following Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported he had an affair with a second employee. Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese operative has raised questions about what he knew about Nvidia’s advanced chips making their way into China despite US export restrictions. Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, but The New York Times reported that, according to third-party data, a subsidiary of Megaspeed “received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia AI technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips,” which were subject to export restrictions. On the heels of Tuesday’s earnings, Nvidia’s stock rose in after-hours trading. The company had lost more than $1 trillion in market value over the past month amid the fallout from Huang’s scandal. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang released his first statement since his resignation. Huang thanked allies for their support, writing he’d “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” He admitted to failing to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia,” adding that he is “committed to cooperating with the board’s independent investigation.” However, Huang concluded, if the board “decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, has roughly 60,000 employees, and sentiments have varied in the wake of Huang’s departure. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” an employee told WIRED last week. But in his 33 years leading Nvidia, Huang earned a loyal army of supporters by minimizing layoffs and red tape. Some employees have been calling for his return to the helm. And a few tech industry heavyweights are similarly eager for Huang to be reinstated. Executives including Elon Musk , Replit CEO Amjad Masad , and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan took to X to voice support for Huang, signing a petition to “Bring Jensen Back.” Huang’s activities are under investigation by at least four entities: the FBI and the US Department of Justice, Congress, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and an independent law firm appointed by Nvidia’s board. Industry sources previously told WIRED that Huang is unlikely to return to the company anytime soon. Interim CEO Kress, at the end of Tuesday’s call, offered what sounded like a rallying cry for anyone doubting Nvidia’s future without Huang. “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed,” Kress said. “We’ve got this.”

sources.title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster
sources.text: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies , export control compliance, and global trade risks. Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff. The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.” Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely. Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue. In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change. Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China. That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch. If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share. stories.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
stories.summary: Turn Gemini’s annotations into an edge model for manufacturing inspection. Explore three prompting approaches, review labels, and train RF-DETR model with Roboflow. Deploy the trained model near the camera and keep Gemini available to inspect difficult cases and improve future training data.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
sources.text: To distill Gemini into an edge model, have Gemini label your images, review and correct those labels, then train a small detector that runs next to the camera and does the routine inspections. In Roboflow, auto-label with Gemini through a class description, the Auto Label agent or an Open Prompt Workflow. Then train RF-DETR Small on the reviewed dataset, run it with Inference on your edge device, and route uncertain cases back to Gemini or a human reviewer. Checking an assembly for missing screws takes more than counting detections. A model might miss one screw and mistake a reflection for another, returning the expected count while overlooking an incomplete product. A useful inspection system needs to locate the visible screws at each mounting position and flag images that need further review. With Roboflow, you can use Gemini to help build the training dataset for that system, then train a compact RF-DETR (opens in a new tab) model to detect screws near the camera. In this approach to model distillation , Gemini generates candidate bounding boxes, you review and correct the annotations, and RF-DETR learns the specific detection task. At deployment, the smaller model handles routine detection, while routing logic sends selected difficult images to Gemini or a person for review. In this guide, you’ll explore three ways to prompt Gemini for screw annotations: class descriptions in Roboflow Auto Label, conversational feedback with the Auto Label agent, and an Open Prompt Workflow that returns boxes for inspection in Python. You’ll then review the labels, train RF-DETR Small, test it on your edge hardware, and configure a fallback for uncertain results. Before generating labels, decide exactly what one object means. In our reference image, each screw annotation covers the full visible fastener region, including its outer exposed end and inner metal feature. One screw receives one box. This definition must stay the same across the dataset. Create an Object Detection project and upload the product images (opens in a new tab) . Include complete products, missing screws, reflections, and realistic changes in lighting. In Roboflow Auto Label (opens in a new tab) , the class description is the prompt Gemini uses to find the object . Follow these steps. Gemini searches using that description, and Auto Label saves each resulting annotation as screw . The expected count of four is an application rule. It should not force the teacher to produce four boxes when a screw is missing. You can also describe the labeling task through Chat with Auto Label agent . The agent builds a labeling Workflow from the model and classes and shows a preview. Use the conversation to refine what it should label. The saved annotations still need a class name, which remains screw in this example. See labeling with the Auto Label agent (opens in a new tab) . With Gemini 4 Carbon selected, open Chat with Auto Label agent and enter the following request. Check the preview and request specific corrections. You can use the following correction when that error appears. You can also click an incorrect label or use Flag missing object. Once the preview matches the annotation rule, choose Use this Workflow, confirm the output-class mapping to screw , and select Label batch. Review the job estimate before starting. Continue with the label review in Section 2. This conversation configures the Auto Label Workflow. Gemini 4 Carbon remains the requested annotation model. Check that the saved Workflow uses it. Either setup option produces the same kind of training data for RF-DETR Small. The training examples contain reviewed screw bounding boxes. For this option, you can choose any Gemini model available in the Roboflow Google Gemini block (opens in a new tab) that supports image input and Open Prompt. You can also try different available models with the same prompt and images to compare their bounding boxes. For the Auto Label process above, Roboflow manages the saved annotations. Use the description field or the Auto Label agent conversation above. Neither option requires you to enter a JSON-format prompt or convert coordinates yourself. If you inspect raw Gemini detection output, Google's official object detection documentation (opens in a new tab) specifies box_2d in [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] order, normalized to 0–1000. Normalization expresses a position relative to the image dimensions. A value of 500 is halfway across the relevant dimension, regardless of image size. Use the following conversion for an image of width W and height H. For example, [100, 200, 300, 250] on a 1000-pixel-wide, 600-pixel-high image gives pixel bounds xmin=200, ymin=60, xmax=250, ymax=180. This is a coordinate example, not a measured screw prediction. Prompting Gemini for boxes in a consistent format gives the visualization code a clear schema to check. Gemini models can still format their answers differently even when they receive the same instructions. This Open Prompt test uses a consistent box_2d schema and a model-independent parser. The prompt requests the screw label and [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] coordinates normalized to 0–1000. The script accepts known JSON formatting differences, but checks the coordinates before drawing them. This follows Gemini’s object-detection coordinate convention (opens in a new tab) . The parser uses the requested coordinate order and scale. Numeric checks alone cannot prove that Gemini followed those instructions, so inspect the drawn boxes. Build this small test separately from Auto Label. Use an image input, a text input for the prompt, one Google Gemini block, and two outputs. Follow Build a Workflow (opens in a new tab) . Test with an assembly image and supply the example text in the Workflow’s prompt input. Confirm that both outputs, boxes_json and prompt_echo , appear in the test response. Save the Workflow and use Deploy (opens in a new tab) to copy its workspace slug, Workflow ID, and API URL for Python. Open Prom

sources.title: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how
sources.text: You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI. Google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI. But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history. Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback. Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road. Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two. To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training. Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes “With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email. Here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats. Almost all AIs include a setting for model training that you typically have to manually disable if you’re concerned about your privacy. But most let you opt out without turning off your chat history. ChatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.” Also: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027 (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.) In all those cases, you still retain access to your conversation history. In contrast, Google has been the only AI player among the majors to impose a restriction for those who want to opt out of AI training. Based on past actions, Google has often earned a reputation for being privacy-unfriendly. I’m glad to see the company take this step in the right direction.
